newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indian sugar sector seen needing reform.
newsitem.headline: Indian sugar sector seen needing reform.

text.p: Sugar remains a political commodity in India 50 years after independence from Britain, and the sector should be deregulated to boost competitiveness, industry sources said on Wednesday.

"Millions of sugarcane farmers constitute a large vote bank, which the political party in power seeks to woo by declaring unrealistically high state-advised sugarcane prices," S.L. Jain, director-general of the Indian Sugar Mills Association said.
"The sugar industry has thus become a pawn in the game of politics," he told an international sugar conference on the island of Bali.
"It's only under a deregulated economy that the sugar industry...will be able to face unequal competition from the traditional alternate sweeteners," he added.

Satish Kansal, general manager of Siel Ltd of India, told the conference that the country's sugar sector remained insulated despite the disappearance of state protection in other industries after economic reforms launched in 1991.
Several regulatory measures still existed at the federal and state government levels that controlled the industry, he said.
Kansal said, however, the government had been encouraging new sugar mills and expansions. He said there were currently 440 mills in India.

He said Indian per capita consumption of sugar and traditional sweeteners such as gur and khandsari was 24 kg per annum, compared with 15 kg in Indonesia, 43 kg in Malaysia, 25 kg in the Philippines and a world average of 20 kg.
Kansal said average yearly demand was around 13.5 million tonnes. He said in the past 15 years India had imported 6.60 million tonnes of sugar and exported 4.50 million.

The Indian Sugar Mills Association's Jain said Indian sugar consumption in 1990-91 (October/September) to 1995-96 increased by 2.6 million tonnes to 14.3 million tonnes from 11.6 million, accounting for one-third of the rise in Asian and global use.
He said Indian sugar consumption had been spurred by lower prices. "The government policies all through history...have been so attuned as to keep prices to the barest minimum," he added.
Jain said there had been no perceptible change in the government approach on regulating the sector though it had begun to liberalise the economy.
He said sugar output was expected to decline to 13 million tonnes in 1996/97 from 16.5 million in 1994-95 and to about 11 million tonnes in 1997-98. He gave no data for 1995/96.
"The steep decline in production...has once again underlined the basic weakness in the sugar policy," he said.

Jain said futures trading in sugar must be permitted in India and exchanges established. He said futures trading was permitted in the 1940s but was banned for fear of an abrupt increase in prices after World War Two.
